reviewer.role: Sports Science and Concurrent Training Reviewer (SSCTR), acting as decision author
reviewer.instance: A subagent instance dispatched by the Chief of this mission (model claude-opus-5-5). Whether it ran through the project native adapter cannot be verified from inside the run.
reviewer.nature: An AI software reviewer. It holds no human credentials, licence, degree or registration and has no clinical or legal equivalence. This record is an internal literature-based decision, not human validation, empirical product validation or medical clearance.
reviewer.independence: This instance authors the values below. It must not judge the implemented candidate; a fresh SSCTR instance does that later (SSCTR-08).

authority: PROVISIONAL_INTERNAL_DOMAIN_AUTHORITY for bounded nonclinical sporting decisions only. Clinical judgment stays CLINICAL_HUMAN_REQUIRED. No runtime sovereignty, no publication of Product Truth, no gate closure by this record.

counterevidenceSearch: Directed: (1) whether intensity progression raises injury risk in recreational runners (Run Clever: no clear difference, wide intervals; participants had at least 6 months of running, so novices are not covered); (2) whether precise interval or long-run recommendations are evidence-based (Midgley 2007: direct evidence insufficient; ladder values are therefore implementation choices inside an envelope, not optimal doses); (3) whether a 3-week marathon taper is too long (Smyth 2021, observational: longer strict tapers up to 3 weeks were associated with better times; Bosquet 2007: 2 weeks optimal in competitive athletes, mostly other sports); (4) whether easy running speeds post-marathon recovery (Sherman 1983/1984: it did not, and work capacity recovered later with running). No source was found that supports a long run above 3 h for recreational runners as necessary; none was found that shows a 3 h cap to be harmful.

sources.citation: Bosquet L, Montpetit J, Arvisais D, Mujika I. Effects of tapering on performance: a meta-analysis. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2007;39(8):1358-65.
sources.findingsUsed: 27 studies of competitive athletes; a 2-week taper with training volume reduced exponentially by 41-60%, intensity and frequency maintained, was the most efficient strategy.

sources.citation: Mujika I, Padilla S. Scientific bases for precompetition tapering strategies. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2003;35(7):1182-7.
sources.findingsUsed: Maintain intensity, reduce volume, reduce frequency by no more than 20%; progressive nonlinear tapers beat step tapers; duration 4 to more than 28 days.

sources.citation: Smyth B, Lawlor A. Longer Disciplined Tapers Improve Marathon Performance for Recreational Runners. Front Sports Act Living 2021;3:735220.
sources.locator: Abstract; Methods (taper profile definitions: strict = consecutive down weeks immediately before race day); Limitations
sources.findingsUsed: More than 158,000 recreational marathoners (app data): strict tapers associated with better performance than relaxed ones; tapers up to 3 weeks associated with better performance than shorter ones; strict 3-week tapers best (median 2.6% finish-time saving versus minimal taper).
limitations: ability proxy from fastest training 10 km

sources.citation: Rasmussen CH, Nielsen RO, Juul MS, Rasmussen S. Weekly running volume and risk of running-related injuries among marathon runners. Int J Sports Phys Ther 2013;8(2):111-20.
sources.findingsUsed: 662 marathon finishers; adjusted for previous injury and previous marathons, running below 30 km/week before the marathon was associated with about twice the injury risk (RR 2.02, 95% CI 1.26-3.24) compared with 30-60 km/week; authors advise at least 30 km/week before a marathon.
limitations: volume averaged over the preparation, not at its start

sources.citation: Videbaek S, Bueno AM, Nielsen RO, Rasmussen S. Incidence of Running-Related Injuries Per 1000 h of running in Different Types of Runners: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Sports Med 2015;45(7):1017-26.
sources.findingsUsed: Weighted incidence 17.8 injuries per 1000 h in novice runners versus 7.7 in recreational runners.

sources.citation: Frandsen JSB, Hulme A, Parner ET, et al. How much running is too much? Identifying high-risk running sessions in a 5200-person cohort study. Br J Sports Med 2025.
sources.locator: Abstract; What this study adds; Exposure; Limitations
sources.findingsUsed: 5205 adult runners, 588,071 sessions: a single session longer than 10% above the longest run of the previous 30 days was associated with a higher rate of overuse injury (small spike HRR 1.64); weekly ACWR and week-to-week ratios were not, or inversely.
limitations: distance, not time; the engine uses time

sources.citation: van Poppel D, van der Worp M, Slabbekoorn A, et al. Risk factors for overuse injuries in short- and long-distance running: A systematic review. J Sport Health Sci 2021;10(1):14-28.
sources.findingsUsed: In long-distance runners a previous running-related injury is the strongest risk factor (moderate-quality evidence); for short-distance runners no previous running experience and lower volume are risk factors; overall quality of risk-factor evidence is limited and injuries are multifactorial.

sources.citation: Sherman WM, Armstrong LE, Murray TM, et al. Effect of a 42.2-km footrace and subsequent rest or exercise on muscular strength and work capacity. J Appl Physiol 1984;57(6):1668-73.
sources.findingsUsed: 10 trained men after a marathon, randomized to a rest week or 20-45 min/day of running: leg work capacity recovered by day 3 with rest but was still impaired at day 7 with running; strength recovery was impaired through days 5-7 after 40-45 min runs.

sources.citation: Sherman WM, Costill DL, Fink WJ, et al. Effect of a 42.2-km footrace and subsequent rest or exercise on muscle glycogen and enzymes. J Appl Physiol 1983;55(4):1219-24.
sources.findingsUsed: Low-intensity running in the recovery week did not differ from rest on glycogen and enzymes; glycogen not fully restored at day 7 in either group.

sources.citation: Hikida RS, Staron RS, Hagerman FC, Sherman WM, Costill DL. Muscle fiber necrosis associated with human marathon runners. J Neurol Sci 1983;59(2):185-203.
sources.findingsUsed: Fiber necrosis and inflammation most prevalent 1-3 days after a marathon and persisting through the 7-day observation window.

sources.citation: Hottenrott K, Ludyga S, Schulze S, Gronwald T, Jager FS. Does a run/walk strategy decrease cardiac stress during a marathon in non-elite runners? J Sci Med Sport 2016;19(1):64-8.
sources.findingsUsed: 42 non-elite runners: run/walk and run-only finished in similar times (about 4h14 vs 4h08); run/walk gave less muscle discomfort; cardiac biomarker rise was similar and reversible.

sources.citation: Ramskov D, Rasmussen S, Sorensen H, Parner ET, Lind M, Nielsen R. Progression in Running Intensity or Running Volume and the Development of Specific Injuries in Recreational Runners: Run Clever, a Randomized Trial Using Competing Risks. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 2018;48(10):740-748.
sources.findingsUsed: 447 healthy recreational runners (inclusion: 1-3 runs/week for the past 6 months, design paper PMID 27107810): progressing weekly running at 88% VO2max or more did not clearly change the risk of intensity-related injuries versus volume progression (risk differences near zero, wide CIs).

sources.citation: Seiler S, Hetlelid KJ. The impact of rest duration on work intensity and RPE during interval training. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2005;37(9):1601-7.
sources.findingsUsed: Self-paced high-intensity intervals: rest between 1 and 4 min had limited effect on self-selected work intensity; about 2 min active recovery was a reasonable balance.

sources.citation: Billat LV. Interval training for performance: a scientific and empirical practice. Part I: aerobic interval training. Sports Med 2001;31(1):13-31.
sources.findingsUsed: Coaches calibrate interval training from 800 m to 5000 m competition velocities; interval work at or above maximal lactate steady state is the established event-specific practice.

sources.citation: Midgley AW, McNaughton LR, Jones AM. Training to enhance the physiological determinants of long-distance running performance. Sports Med 2007;37(10):857-80.
sources.findingsUsed: COUNTEREVIDENCE: direct evidence is insufficient to give valid precise training recommendations to distance runners.

sources.citation: Blagrove RC, Howatson G, Hayes PR. Effects of Strength Training on the Physiological Determinants of Middle- and Long-Distance Running Performance: A Systematic Review. Sports Med 2018;48(5):1117-1149.
sources.findingsUsed: Strength training added to running generally improved running economy (2-8%) and time-trial performance in runners with at least 6 months of experience.

sources.citation: Spiering BA, Mujika I, Sharp MA, Foulis SA. Maintaining Physical Performance: The Minimal Dose of Exercise Needed to Preserve Endurance and Strength Over Time. J Strength Cond Res 2021;35(5):1449-1458.
sources.findingsUsed: Strength and size maintained for long periods with 1 session/week and 1 set/exercise if relative load is kept; endurance maintained with volume reduced 33-66% if intensity is kept.

sources.citation: McGowan CJ, Pyne DB, Thompson KG, Rattray B. Warm-Up Strategies for Sport and Exercise: Mechanisms and Applications. Sports Med 2015;45(11):1523-46.
sources.findingsUsed: Active warm-up improves preparedness for subsequent exercise; specific warm-up durations rest largely on practice rather than direct evidence.

sources.citation: Schwellnus M, Adami PE, Bougault V, et al. International Olympic Committee (IOC) consensus statement on acute respiratory illness in athletes part 1: acute respiratory infections. Br J Sports Med 2022;56(19):1066-1088.
sources.access: RECORD and abstract re-confirmed 2026-11-11; full-text postprint was read by SSCTR-V1CP-DECISION-r1 (its S06), not re-read here
sources.findingsUsed: Return after acute respiratory infection is a symptom-guided continuum; red-flag symptoms need professional assessment (as summarized in SSCTR-V1CP-DECISION-r1 S06).

globalConditions.condition: Existing events are unchanged: with a 10K or half-marathon goal, every output stays byte-identical to the current candidate (3b14804). Show it with a differential on the existing suites. 10K and half keep taperWeeks 1.

Every existing safety and progression rule applies to the 5K and the marathon unchanged: clinical screen first, ADVANCE/HOLD/REGRESS on executed sessions, singleRunCeiling (longest completed run in 30 days + 5), longRunShareOfWeeklyMinutesMax 0.45 (holds, never shortens), first-week rules, consolidation every 4th development week, mode-aware event sessions, raceDateUnavailable (asked, never kept or skipped silently), achievedPeakBasis, longRunFloor, postRaceEligibility and the restart history reset.

The race session never counts as an achieved long, easy or quality peak, never counts toward the longest continuous run statement as a training run, and never becomes the singleRunCeiling reference for taper, post-event or next-block doses. Prove it with a marathon test (a 240-minute race must not set the next block's long run). This applies to every event.
No pace, zone, VO2max, threshold or finish-time claim or prediction for any event. Effort cues only.

Catalog status changes only as this record states: LATER.EVENT.5K becomes the reviewed 5K recipe; UNSUPPORTED.EVENT.MARATHON_ULTRA becomes bounded marathon support (ultra stays UNSUPPORTED_V1); LATER.RUN.MULTI_WEEK_TAPER becomes 2 taper weeks for the marathon only; LATER.RUN.VO2_DE_NOVO stays LATER_GATE (the 5K ladder is effort-cued event work, not a VO2 path).
An executed race longer than its race-day window is never an adverse response, a non-adherence signal or a reason for a gate change; the window is a planning upper bound only.
A fresh SSCTR instance judges the implemented candidate against this record before any readiness claim.

conditions: The warning-sign instrument is unchanged: every item actively answered, unknown is ASK (never the unavailability), any yes routes CLINICAL_HUMAN_REQUIRED for every sport.
The report is recorded append-only. It never counts as a compatible response, never feeds ADVANCE or EARNED, and is never presented as 'safe' or 'cleared'.

Situation 1 state is unreachable from every input (app, legacy or imported record), not only hidden in the UI. Tests: each S1 intent yields the typed unavailability and a plan byte-identical to the one before the report.
QRE-FFC-01's mechanism (the D49 cap lost across a per-sport chain) is shown unreachable through the kept paths: a per-sport chain of declared breaks keeps the D49 cap.

The typed unavailability tells the athlete: (1) the app does not adjust the plan for feeling under par in this version; (2) you may skip, shorten or stop any session; a missed session is never made up and the plan does not step up on sessions not done; (3) if you need days off, declare a break and the return is planned for you; (4) if symptoms persist or worsen, or any warning sign appears, report it and seek a health professional's assessment; (5) if the race is within 20 days, you can mark the race date unavailable or change the event. It never says you are fine to train.
items.rationale: No athlete gets a less safe path than the validated state. Warning signs still route to the clinical hold; an illness reason on a declared break is a clinical category and goes to the hold with the MODERATE restart, which is more conservative than S1's illness rungs; executed-session gates still hold or regress after adverse responses.
